clinicalPearls: Renal scarring resulting from vesicoureteric reflux, typically with childhood urinary tract infections
It is an important cause of chronic kidney disease and of hypertension in children and young adults
Characteristic imaging shows focal cortical scars overlying dilated calyces, often at the poles
It may present with hypertension, proteinuria, recurrent infections or incidentally reduced renal function
Established scarring is irreversible, so prevention and early detection are key
Management focuses on blood pressure and proteinuria control and prevention of further infection and scarring
reference.pathophysiology: Reflux nephropathy develops when vesicoureteric reflux, particularly with intrarenal reflux and urinary infection during early childhood, damages the renal parenchyma and produces focal scarring. The scars disrupt nephrons and, once a critical amount of renal mass is affected, trigger hyperfiltration injury in the remaining nephrons, causing progressive proteinuria, glomerulosclerosis and declining function. Activation of the renin-angiotensin system contributes to the associated hypertension, which further accelerates renal injury.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of chronic kidney disease with scarring
additionalInvestigations: Renal ultrasound and DMSA scintigraphy for scarring
Assessment of blood pressure, proteinuria and renal function
Micturating cystourethrography where active reflux is investigated
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the extent of scarring; limited disease may remain stable, but extensive bilateral scarring can progress to end-stage kidney disease, especially with uncontrolled hypertension or proteinuria.
pitfalls: Failing to control hypertension and proteinuria that drive progression
Attributing the scarring purely to infection without recognising reflux
Overlooking reflux nephropathy as a cause of young-adult hypertension
